scenes.script_line: Before we look at what isn't working, we start somewhere else. With what matters most to you. Why start here? Because you can't change a story well if you don't know where you want to go. Step one gives the whole process its direction. Everything you write later will be measured against what you write here.

shots.text: wide shot of a person looking out over a view, thinking ahead
close-up of a blank workbook page waiting to be filled
person sitting at a table, pen in hand, about to begin
shots.pexels: person at table pen in hand

scenes.script_line: So, what inspires you about what's ahead? This includes your dreams, your aspirations, and the direction your life is drawing you toward, both in the short term and the long term. Pay attention to what consistently pulls at you. What excites you. What energises you. What feels deeply meaningful. These things usually point to something deeper about who you are.

shots.text: person with eyes closed, picturing something meaningful
person smiling gently while watching family across a room
close-up of hands holding a pen, about to write
shots.pexels: hands holding pen about to write

scenes.script_line: Think across your whole life, not just one part of it. Your work. Your relationships. Your health. Your growth. And the difference you want to make for others. On page six, you'll write between three and fifteen clear statements about what matters most to you moving forward. Two simple rules. First, make them clear. Not "be happier," but "spend unhurried evenings with my family." Second, write them in the positive. Not "stop being stressed about money," but "feel calm and in control of my finances." Your mind moves toward what you focus on, so describe what you want, not what you want to avoid

shots.text: person writing a list in a workbook at a kitchen table
close-up of a hand crossing out a word and rewriting it
wide shot of a quiet home at evening, unhurried

scenes.script_line: Let's look at an example. Meet Sam. Sam's list includes statements like these. "I lead a team I'm proud of." "I share my ideas with confidence." "I have energy for the people I love at the end of the day." Simple, clear, and positive. Two things to watch for. First, don't write what other people expect of you. If a statement starts to sound like "I should," pause and ask whether it's truly yours. Second, check how each one feels. Read it back. If it gives you a little lift of energy, it belongs on your list. If it feels heavy, it may belong to someone else.

shots.text: person reading their own written list back to themselves
close-up of a face lighting up slightly while reading a line
shots.pexels: face lighting up reading line close up

shots.text: person pausing, pen down, weighing a heavier line

scenes.script_line: Then there's a second part to this step. Your Destiny Scroll. This takes the long view. Imagine you've reached the end of a long and full life. Someone who knows you deeply looks back on it and says: "Your life was one that…" How would you want that sentence to end? Think about what you stood for. How others were changed because you were in their lives. The deeper significance your life carried.

shots.text: older person looking back thoughtfully, warm light
close-up of a hand writing a short, careful sentence
wide shot of a person sitting alone in quiet reflection

scenes.script_line: Complete that summary in no more than three lines. Keep it short. The limit forces you to choose what truly matters. Sam wrote: "Your life was one that helped others believe in themselves, because you learned to believe in yourself." Don't worry about getting it perfect. This is a first draft of your direction, and you can return to it at any time. Your facilitator will guide you as you write your statements and your Destiny Scroll.
